title: Episode 4 (lines 753–883)

teacherSummary.text: Antigone is led toward her living tomb. She laments “Unwept, unwed, unfriended, hence I go” (line 819), compares herself to the daughter of Tantalus (Niobe in myth, though the play does not name her), and argues that a brother, once both parents are dead, can never be replaced. The Chorus both pities and reproaches her. Creon orders the guards to take her away.

anchorPassages.note: Lament joins personal doom to the Labdacid curse and the brother she buried.
anchorPassages.text:
O fount of Dirce, wood-embowered plain
Where Theban chariots to victory speed,
Mark ye the cruel laws that now have wrought my bane,
The friends who show no pity in my need!
Was ever fate like mine? O monstrous doom,
Within a rock-built prison sepulchred,
To fade and wither in a living tomb,
An alien midst the living and the dead.
In thy boldness over-rash
Madly thou thy foot didst dash
’Gainst high Justice’ altar stair.
Thou a father’s guilt dost bear.
At this thou touchest my most poignant pain,
My ill-starred father’s piteous disgrace,
The taint of blood, the hereditary stain,
That clings to all of Labdacus’ famed race.
Woe worth the monstrous marriage-bed where lay
A mother with the son her womb had borne;
Therein I was conceived, woe worth the day,
Fruit of incestuous sheets, a maid forlorn,
And now I pass, accursèd and unwed,
To meet them as an alien there below;
And thee, O brother, in marriage ill-bestead,
’Twas thy dead hand that dealt me this death-blow.

anchorPassages.note: Creon's legal fiction of non-bloodshed while walling her into death.
anchorPassages.text:
Unwept, unwed, unfriended, hence I go,
No longer may I see the day’s bright eye;
Not one friend left to share my bitter woe,
And o’er my ashes heave one passing sigh.
If wail and lamentation aught availed
To stave off death, I trow they’d never end.
Away with her, and having walled her up
In a rock-vaulted tomb, as I ordained,
Leave her alone at liberty to die,
Or, if she choose, to live in solitude,
The tomb her dwelling. We in either case
Are guiltless as concerns this maiden’s blood.
Only on earth no lodging shall she find.

anchorPassages.note: Famous casuistry of the irreplaceable brother, then the cry that piety itself is deemed crime.
anchorPassages.text:
O grave, O bridal bower, O prison house
Hewn from the rock, my everlasting home,
Whither I go to join the mighty host
Of kinsfolk, Persephassa’s guests long dead,
The last of all, of all most miserable,
I pass, my destined span of years cut short.
And yet good hope is mine that I shall find
A welcome from my sire, a welcome too,
From thee, my mother, and my brother dear;
For with these hands, I laved and decked your limbs
In death, and poured libations on your grave.
And last, my Polyneices, unto thee
I paid due rites, and this my recompense!
Yet am I justified in wisdom’s eyes.
For even had it been some child of mine,
Or husband mouldering in death’s decay,
I had not wrought this deed despite the State.
What is the law I call in aid? ’Tis thus
I argue. Had it been a husband dead
I might have wed another, and have borne
Another child, to take the dead child’s place.
But, now my sire and mother both are dead,
No second brother can be born for me.
Thus by the law of conscience I was led
To honour thee, dear brother, and was judged
By Creon guilty of a heinous crime.
And now he drags me like a criminal,
A bride unwed, amerced of marriage-song
And marriage-bed and joys of motherhood,
By friends deserted to a living grave.

anchorPassages.note: Exit to death: the last of the royal house claims martyrdom before the city.
anchorPassages.text:
What ordinance of heaven have I transgressed?
Hereafter can I look to any god
For succour, call on any man for help?
Alas, my piety is impious deemed.
Well, if such justice is approved of heaven,
I shall be taught by suffering my sin;
But if the sin is theirs, O may they suffer
No worse ills than the wrongs they do to me!
The same ungovernable will
Drives like a gale the maiden still.
Therefore, my guards who let her stay
Shall smart full sore for their delay.
Ah, woe is me! This word I hear
Brings death most near.
I have no comfort. What he saith,
Portends no other thing than death.
My fatherland, city of Thebes divine,
Ye gods of Thebes whence sprang my line,
Look, puissant lords of Thebes, on me;
The last of all your royal house ye see.
Martyred by men of sin, undone.
Such meed my piety hath won. Exit Antigone.

weDoAnswers: Goethe, in conversation with Eckermann, wished the brother argument (lines 849–854) could be removed (Eckermann, 1850, entry of March 28, 1827). It is part of the text and is taught in full. Read closely: “Religion has her claims, ’tis true, Let rites be paid when rites are due. Yet is it ill to disobey The powers who hold by might the sway. Thou hast withstood authority, A self-willed rebel, thou must die.” (Chorus, lines 813–818).
analysis.weDoWords: “Claims”, “rites” and “self-willed rebel” stand out in lines 813–818. The elders grant that religion has its claims, and that rites should be paid when they are due, but they still call Antigone a rebel against power, so their judgment is divided. “Self-willed rebel, thou must die” closes the grant with a sentence.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Was ever fate like mine? O monstrous doom, / Within a rock-built prison sepulchred, / To fade and wither in a living tomb, / An alien midst the living and the dead” slowly and put it in my own words: Antigone asks whether any fate has been like hers, to be buried in a rock prison, to wither in a living tomb, belonging neither to the living nor to the dead. Next, craft. “Sepulchred” and “living tomb” turn the cave into a burial while she still breathes, and “alien midst the living and the dead” names the in-between place the sentence creates. The strongest word is “sepulchred”: it buries her in the wording while she is still speaking. Then, effect. What do lines 793–796 reveal about Antigone's farewell? My answer: Antigone’s farewell shows a defiant heroine who is also a young woman afraid to die. Her lament makes her more human, not less; the wording lets us hear the cost of the stand she has already taken.

On theme: Her argument that a brother cannot be replaced once both parents are dead tests how far family piety can justify breaking the city’s law. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

items.text: Does Antigone's brother argument (849–854) strengthen or weaken her case? Argue with evidence.
items.lookFor: A defended position, strengthen or weaken, that quotes lines 846–854.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A strong answer can say the argument weakens her case: she claims that, had it been a husband or child, she would not have defied the State, because another husband or child could replace them, whereas no second brother can be born (lines 846–854). Goethe wished these lines removed; they are taught as part of the text. A strong answer can also say it strengthens her case by naming the unique family bond that the unwritten laws protect. Either view must quote the lines.

items.text: The Chorus tells Antigone that she bears a father's guilt. Is it fair to hold her family's past against her? Defend your view.
items.lookFor: A defended position.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defended position.

items.text: Creon says the city stays guiltless of the maiden's blood (lines 825–830). Does this reasoning hold? Argue with evidence.
items.lookFor: A defended position on Creon’s “guiltless” claim (lines 825–830), with evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Creon claims that, whether she dies or lives in the tomb, “We in either case / Are guiltless as concerns this maiden’s blood” (lines 829–830). A strong answer can reject this: he still walls her up “In a rock-vaulted tomb” (lines 825–826) and leaves her no lodging on earth (line 831), so the city is not outside the deed. A contrasting view can note that he offers her a choice to live in solitude rather than a direct public execution. Evidence from these lines is required.

O monstrous doom, / Within a rock-built prison sepulchred, / To fade and wither in a living tomb, / An alien midst the living and the dead” (Episode 4, lines 793–796): Antigone, lines 793–796. On characterization: Antigone’s farewell mixes defiance with fear: “Unwept, unwed, unfriended, hence I go” (line 819), yet she still argues the irreplaceable claim of a brother. items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The defiant heroine is also a young woman afraid to die. Her lament makes her more human, not less. Useful evidence: “Religion has her claims, ’tis true, / Let rites be paid when rites are due. / Yet is it ill to disobey / The powers who hold by might the sway. / Thou hast withstood authority” (Episode 4, lines 813–818): Chorus, lines 813–818. Theme link: The Chorus grants that “Religion has her claims” but still calls Antigone a “self-willed rebel” who must die, so human authority is set above the rite she honoured. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.
